paragraphs.heading: An army built from scratch
paragraphs.text: When the Revolutionary War opened at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775, the rebelling colonists had no standing army to call on. Until then each colony had leaned on its militia, a body of part-time citizen-soldiers who guarded their own area. In wartime a colony might also raise provincial troops for a limited stretch, as happened in the French and Indian War. As trouble with Britain grew, colonists began reorganizing their militias, and training stepped up after the Intolerable Acts of 1774.

paragraphs.heading: Founding in 1775
paragraphs.text: Richard Henry Lee had suggested a national militia, but the First Continental Congress turned the idea down. On June 14, 1775, the Second Continental Congress, sitting in Philadelphia, voted to create the Continental Army for the shared defense of the colonies against Britain. It took in the New England Army of Observation already camped outside Boston and the forces around New York City. The same day, Congress unanimously chose George Washington as Commander in Chief.

paragraphs.heading: Washington in command
paragraphs.text: Washington accepted, went straight to Boston, and led a siege of the city that succeeded. He stayed in command for the whole war and took no pay, only repayment of his expenses. The army drew its soldiers from the colonies and, after 1776, from the United States. State troops and volunteer militia filled out its ranks from time to time.

paragraphs.heading: Debate and reform
paragraphs.text: Some Americans disliked the idea of a standing army on principle. Yet the war seemed to demand the discipline and organization of a central military. So the army kept changing, reorganizing its units again and again, and in the end it won support from France, which wanted to push back British influence in North America. Military business was first handled by the whole Congress, then by a standing Board of War and Ordnance set up in June 1776.

paragraphs.heading: Fixing the enlistment problem
paragraphs.text: The first troops enlisted for just one year, so the army faced a crisis each time a year closed and terms ran out. At the end of 1776 it nearly collapsed this way, which could have lost the war by simple default. Congress passed the Eighty-eight Battalion Resolve, which ordered each state to supply regiments in proportion to its population. To avoid those year-end crises, enlistments were stretched to three years or for as long as the war lasted.

paragraphs.heading: The hardest years
paragraphs.text: The years 1781 and 1782 brought the gravest crisis on the American side. Congress had run out of money, so it struggled to replace soldiers whose three-year terms had ended. Public backing for the war fell to its lowest point, and Washington had to put down mutinies in the Pennsylvania Line and the New Jersey Line. Even with its funding cut, the army under Washington still won important strategic victories.

paragraphs.heading: Disbanding and legacy
paragraphs.text: Once peace with Britain returned, most regiments were sent home in an orderly way. Congress disbanded the army on June 2, 1784, keeping only small groups of privates at Fort Pitt, West Point and other military storehouses, plus a small artillery unit. The force that followed it was the United States Army, which still exists today.
